disease.name: Appendicitis
disease.scientific_name: Acute Appendicitis / Inflammation of the Vermiform Appendix
disease.icd_10_code: K35-K37 (K35.2: Acute appendicitis with generalized peritonitis; K35.3: with localized peritonitis; K36: Other appendicitis; K37: Unspecified appendicitis)

overview.description: Appendicitis is the acute inflammation of the vermiform appendix — a small, finger-shaped pouch attached to the cecum at the junction of the small and large intestine in the right lower quadrant (RLQ) of the abdomen. It is the most common surgical emergency worldwide, affecting approximately 7-8% of the population over a lifetime. Obstruction of the appendix lumen — most commonly by a fecalith (hardened stool), lymphoid hyperplasia, or foreign body — leads to bacterial overgrowth, increased intraluminal pressure, vascular compromise, and ultimately inflammation, gangrene, and perforation if untreated. Prompt diagnosis and surgical management (appendectomy) is lifesaving.
overview.affected_organ: Vermiform Appendix (cecal appendix) — located in the right iliac fossa (RIF) / right lower quadrant (RLQ) of the abdomen
overview.prevalence: Lifetime risk: 7-8% in Western populations; approximately 300,000 appendectomies performed annually in the USA; most common abdominal surgical emergency globally.
overview.age_group: Predominantly affects individuals aged 10-30 years (peak 15-25 years); can occur at any age; less common in infants and elderly (but more dangerous when it does).

anatomy_and_physiology.appendix_location: Vermiform appendix arises from the posteromedial aspect of the cecum, approximately 2-3 cm below the ileocecal valve. Most commonly positioned retrocecal (65-70%), pelvic (25-30%), subcecal, preileal, or paracolic. Position variation explains varied pain presentation.
anatomy_and_physiology.blood_supply: Appendicular artery — branch of the ileocolic artery (from superior mesenteric artery). Terminal blood supply — obstruction leads rapidly to ischemia.
anatomy_and_physiology.function: The appendix contains lymphoid tissue (part of GALT — gut-associated lymphoid tissue). Previously considered vestigial; now thought to act as a 'safe house' for gut bacteria, involved in immune function in early life.
anatomy_and_physiology.mcburneys_point: McBurney's point is the classic location of maximal tenderness in appendicitis — located 1/3 of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus. The surface marking of the base of the appendix.

types.name: Acute Simple (Uncomplicated) Appendicitis
types.description: Early stage inflammation of the appendix mucosa and wall without perforation, gangrene, or abscess. The appendix is edematous, hyperemic, and may have a fibrinous exudate on the serosa. This is the ideal stage for surgical intervention — lowest complication rate.
types.pathology: Mucosal ulceration, transmural neutrophilic infiltration, vascular congestion
types.management: Urgent laparoscopic or open appendectomy; OR non-operative management (antibiotics alone) in selected cases per newer evidence
types.prognosis: Excellent with prompt treatment; complications rare

types.name: Suppurative (Phlegmonous) Appendicitis
types.description: Progressive stage where the entire appendix wall is infiltrated with pus-forming bacteria. The appendix becomes distended with mucopurulent contents. Pus may be visible on the serosal surface. Increased risk of complications.
types.pathology: Full-thickness suppurative inflammation; fibrinopurulent periappendiceal exudate

types.name: Gangrenous Appendicitis
types.description: Advanced stage where blood supply to the appendix is compromised due to thrombosis of appendicular vessels, leading to ischemia and tissue necrosis (gangrene). The appendix wall becomes black/green, friable, and may have focal full-thickness necrosis. Perforation is imminent.
types.pathology: Vascular thrombosis, coagulative necrosis, transmural gangrene, patchy full-thickness necrosis
types.management: Emergency appendectomy; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics; higher risk of post-operative complications
types.prognosis: Guarded without treatment; good with prompt surgery though higher morbidity than simple appendicitis

types.name: Perforated Appendicitis
types.description: The gangrenous appendix ruptures, releasing fecal contents and bacteria into the peritoneal cavity. Can cause localized peritonitis (contained by omentum and bowel) or diffuse generalized peritonitis (surgical emergency with high mortality risk). Perforation occurs in 20-30% of all appendicitis cases overall; 40-70% in children under 5 and elderly over 65.
types.pathology: Full-thickness perforation; peritoneal contamination with enteric organisms
types.risk_factors_for_perforation: Delay in presentation (>24-48 hours), extremes of age (infants, elderly), immunocompromised, atypical presentation delaying diagnosis
types.management: Emergency surgery; aggressive IV broad-spectrum antibiotics; fluid resuscitation; drainage of abscess if present
types.prognosis: Significantly worse than uncomplicated; mortality 0.5-5% in adults; higher in elderly

types.name: Appendiceal Abscess (Periappendiceal Abscess)
types.description: A localized collection of pus around a perforated appendix, walled off by the omentum, peritoneum, and adjacent bowel loops forming a phlegmon or abscess. The body's attempt to contain peritoneal contamination. Presents as a palpable RLQ mass with prolonged symptoms.
types.pathology: Localized periappendiceal suppuration; fibrous walling by omentum and mesentery
types.management: Image-guided percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics; interval appendectomy at 6-8 weeks (optional and controversial); OR immediate appendectomy in experienced centers
types.prognosis: Good with appropriate management; recurrence risk 5-10% without interval appendectomy

types.name: Chronic / Recurrent Appendicitis
types.description: A controversial entity characterized by recurrent mild episodes of RLQ pain lasting weeks to months, with spontaneous resolution. Believed to result from partial luminal obstruction, low-grade inflammation, or fibrosis of the appendiceal wall. Each episode may be self-limiting but risk of acute progression remains.
types.pathology: Chronic fibrosis of appendiceal wall; partial luminal obstruction; intermittent low-grade inflammation
types.management: Elective appendectomy after thorough investigation to exclude other causes of recurrent RLQ pain (ovarian cyst, IBS, Crohn's disease)
types.prognosis: Excellent with elective appendectomy; risk of acute flare until appendix removed

types.name: Stump Appendicitis
types.description: Rare but dangerous — appendicitis occurring in a residual appendiceal stump left behind after a previous appendectomy. Often misdiagnosed because clinicians do not consider appendicitis in a patient who has had their appendix removed. Delayed diagnosis leads to perforation.
types.note: Prevented by ensuring complete appendiceal removal at time of appendectomy

types.name: Appendicitis Secondary to Neoplasm
types.description: Appendiceal tumors — most commonly carcinoid tumors (neuroendocrine tumors — most common appendix neoplasm, usually <2cm at tip), mucinous neoplasms (LAMN, HAMN), and adenocarcinoma — can obstruct the appendiceal lumen causing secondary appendicitis. Discovered incidentally at histopathology after appendectomy.
types.incidence: Appendiceal tumors found in ~1% of appendectomy specimens; carcinoid (NET) most common
types.management: Simple appendectomy usually curative for carcinoid <2cm; right hemicolectomy for larger tumors or adenocarcinoma; oncology referral

severity_levels.name: Uncomplicated Appendicitis (Simple / Early)
severity_levels.description: Appendiceal inflammation without perforation, gangrene, abscess, or peritonitis
severity_levels.clinical_features: Classic migratory RLQ pain; localized McBurney's point tenderness; low-grade fever (37.5-38.5°C); mild leukocytosis (10,000-18,000/µL)
severity_levels.imaging: Non-perforated appendix on CT/ultrasound; appendiceal diameter 6-12 mm; periappendiceal fat stranding
severity_levels.management: Urgent appendectomy (laparoscopic preferred) within 6-12 hours of diagnosis; single-dose prophylactic IV antibiotics (cefazolin + metronidazole); OR non-operative management (antibiotics only) in carefully selected adults

severity_levels.name: Complicated Appendicitis — Gangrenous
severity_levels.description: Appendiceal wall ischemia and necrosis without complete perforation
severity_levels.clinical_features: More severe pain; higher fever (38-39°C); higher leukocytosis (15,000-25,000/µL); guarding; peritonism
severity_levels.imaging: Appendiceal wall enhancement defect on CT; periappendiceal fluid; appendiceal diameter typically >12mm
severity_levels.management: Emergency appendectomy; perioperative broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone + metronidazole); extended antibiotic course post-op
severity_levels.prognosis: Good with timely surgery; higher complication rate than simple appendicitis

severity_levels.name: Complicated Appendicitis — Perforated with Localized Peritonitis
severity_levels.description: Appendiceal perforation with localized peritoneal contamination; walled off by omentum and bowel; abscess may be present
severity_levels.clinical_features: Prolonged symptoms >24-48 hours; moderate to high fever (38.5-39.5°C); localized RLQ tenderness with guarding; possible palpable mass; WBC 18,000-25,000/µL
severity_levels.imaging: Perforation visible on CT; localized free air; periappendiceal abscess or phlegmon; thickened cecal wall
severity_levels.management: Emergency appendectomy + drainage; OR IR-guided percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + interval appendectomy; fluid resuscitation; prolonged IV antibiotics (5-7 days)
severity_levels.prognosis: Good with appropriate management; longer hospital stay; higher post-operative complication rate

severity_levels.name: Complicated Appendicitis — Perforated with Generalized Peritonitis (CRITICAL EMERGENCY)
severity_levels.description: Rupture with free diffuse spread of fecal contents throughout the peritoneal cavity; diffuse peritonitis; sepsis; life-threatening
severity_levels.clinical_features: Board-like rigid abdomen; diffuse severe abdominal pain and tenderness; high fever (>39°C) or hypothermia in septic shock; tachycardia; hypotension; septic shock; WBC >25,000/µL or paradoxically low in overwhelming sepsis
severity_levels.imaging: Free air under diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) on erect CXR; diffuse peritoneal fluid on CT; severe fat stranding throughout abdomen
severity_levels.management: ICU-level resuscitation; emergency exploratory laparotomy; peritoneal washout; IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam + methotrexate or imipenem-cilastatin); vasopressors if septic shock; prolonged ICU care
severity_levels.prognosis: Guarded; mortality 0.5-2% in adults; up to 20% in elderly with delayed presentation; septic shock increases mortality significantly

causes.primary_cause: Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen leading to bacterial overgrowth, increased intraluminal pressure, vascular compromise, and progressive inflammation.

luminal_obstruction_causes.description: Hardened fecal matter calcified around a nidus (undigested vegetable matter, hair, seeds). Most common cause in adults. Visible on CT as a calcified opacity in the appendix or RLQ.
luminal_obstruction_causes.prevalence: Most common identifiable cause (~40% of cases)

luminal_obstruction_causes.description: Reactive enlargement of lymphoid follicles in the appendiceal submucosa in response to viral or bacterial infection (viral gastroenteritis, Yersinia, Campylobacter, measles, adenovirus, Epstein-Barr virus). Compresses the appendiceal lumen from within.
luminal_obstruction_causes.prevalence: Most common cause in children and adolescents (~60% of pediatric cases)

luminal_obstruction_causes.description: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm/threadworm) — most common parasite causing appendiceal obstruction; worms migrate into appendix. Also Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm). More common in developing countries.
luminal_obstruction_causes.prevalence: Common in endemic areas; found in 1-3% of appendectomy specimens

luminal_obstruction_causes.description: Accidentally swallowed objects (seeds — grape seeds, cherry seeds; fish bones; toothpicks; pins; vegetable matter) that migrate into the appendix and obstruct the lumen.
Carcinoid tumors (neuroendocrine tumors — most at appendiceal tip), mucinous neoplasms (LAMN), or adenocarcinoma obstructing the appendiceal lumen from within or compressing from outside.
luminal_obstruction_causes.prevalence: Found in ~1% of appendectomy specimens; more common in elderly appendicitis

luminal_obstruction_causes.description: External compression of appendiceal lumen by cecal carcinoma, enlarged lymph nodes, Crohn's disease strictures, or adhesions.
luminal_obstruction_causes.prevalence: Rare; important to consider in elderly patients

pathophysiological_sequence: Step 1: Luminal obstruction → bacterial overgrowth of normal gut flora (E. coli, Bacteroides, Enterococcus, anaerobes)
Step 2: Continued mucus secretion against obstruction → rising intraluminal pressure
Step 3: Intraluminal pressure exceeds venous and lymphatic drainage pressure → mucosal ischemia and edema
Step 4: Bacterial invasion of appendiceal wall → acute transmural inflammation (hours 12-24)
Step 5: Arterial thrombosis → gangrene and full-thickness necrosis (hours 24-48)
Step 6: Perforation through necrotic wall → localized or generalized peritonitis (hours 48-72, varies widely)
risk_factors: Male sex — 1.4x higher lifetime risk than females; male-to-female ratio 1.4:1
Age 10-30 years — peak incidence; higher lymphoid tissue content in adolescence
Low-fibre, high-refined-carbohydrate diet — increases fecalith formation; epidemiological evidence
Family history — possible genetic predisposition; studies suggest 3x higher risk with first-degree relative history
Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease) — may cause appendiceal involvement or mimic appendicitis
Previous gastrointestinal infections — lymphoid hyperplasia trigger
Intestinal parasitic infections (endemic areas) — Enterobius vermicularis
genetic_factors: Family history increases risk 3-fold; possible hereditary predisposition to fecalith formation or immune response
Studies show higher concordance in monozygotic vs dizygotic twins
No single gene identified; likely polygenic

primary_symptoms.name: Migratory Abdominal Pain (Periumbilical to RLQ)
primary_symptoms.description: The hallmark symptom of appendicitis. Pain begins as a dull, poorly localized, periumbilical (around the navel) or central abdominal ache — visceral pain from appendiceal distension stimulating T10 afferents. Over 6-24 hours, pain migrates to the right lower quadrant (RLQ) / McBurney's point as the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum — somatic pain, well-localized and sharp. This classic migration occurs in ~50-60% of cases.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild initially → Severe (7-10/10) as peritonitis develops

primary_symptoms.name: Anorexia (Loss of Appetite)
primary_symptoms.description: Loss of appetite is one of the earliest and most consistent symptoms of appendicitis — present in >90% of cases. Characteristically precedes or accompanies the abdominal pain. A patient with acute abdominal pain who is hungry is less likely to have appendicitis.
primary_symptoms.onset: Early — often before or with onset of pain; highly specific when present with RLQ pain

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea and Vomiting
primary_symptoms.description: Nausea follows the onset of pain in appendicitis (pain first, then nausea — opposite pattern to gastroenteritis where vomiting typically precedes or occurs with abdominal pain). Vomiting occurs in 50-80% of cases; usually 1-3 episodes, not profuse. Persistent vomiting suggests perforation or alternative diagnosis.
primary_symptoms.onset: Follows pain onset (pain precedes vomiting — important diagnostic clue)

primary_symptoms.name: Low-Grade Fever
primary_symptoms.description: Temperature typically 37.5-38.5°C (99.5-101.3°F) in uncomplicated appendicitis. Higher fever (>38.5°C) suggests gangrenous or perforated appendicitis, or secondary bacterial peritonitis. Absence of fever does not exclude appendicitis.
primary_symptoms.onset: Several hours after onset of pain

primary_symptoms.name: Right Lower Quadrant (RLQ) Tenderness at McBurney's Point
primary_symptoms.description: Maximal tenderness at McBurney's point (1/3 of the way from the right ASIS to the umbilicus) on palpation is the most important physical examination finding. Rebound tenderness (Blumberg's sign) — pain on rapid release of pressure — indicates peritoneal irritation. Guarding (voluntary or involuntary muscle rigidity) worsens as inflammation progresses.
primary_symptoms.onset: Develops as visceral pain localizes to somatic parietal peritoneum

primary_symptoms.name: Constipation or Diarrhea
primary_symptoms.description: Altered bowel habits are common. Constipation is more frequent. Some patients — especially children and those with pelvic appendix — develop diarrhea from rectal irritation by the inflamed appendix. Significant diarrhea may suggest gastroenteritis but does not exclude appendicitis.
primary_symptoms.onset: Variable; concurrent with or after pain onset

secondary_symptoms: Malaise and general feeling of being unwell
Flushed appearance and dry tongue/mucous membranes (dehydration from reduced intake and fever)
Right-sided groin or testicular pain (if appendix tip in pelvic position irritating right genitofemoral nerve)
Dysuria and urinary frequency (if retrocecal or pelvic appendix lies adjacent to right ureter or bladder)
Diarrhea with tenesmus (if pelvic appendix — may mimic pelvic inflammatory disease in women)
Raised respiratory rate (from abdominal pain splinting diaphragm or sepsis)
Tachycardia (from pain, fever, dehydration, or sepsis)
Peritonism (involuntary muscle guarding, board-like rigidity in perforation)
warning_signs_of_perforation: Sudden brief relief of severe pain followed by rapid worsening and spread of pain throughout the abdomen — classic sign of perforation and peritoneal spill
Rapid rise in temperature to >39°C (>102.2°F) — suggests perforation and bacterial peritonitis
Board-like rigid abdomen with generalized tenderness and guarding — diffuse peritonitis
Signs of septic shock: falling blood pressure, rising heart rate (>120 bpm), cold sweaty extremities, altered consciousness
Abdominal distension and inability to pass flatus — intestinal ileus from peritonitis
Looking severely ill — peritonitis has a toxic appearance: pale, diaphoretic, unable to move without severe pain
symptoms_in_children: Classic migratory pain and anorexia may be poorly communicated by young children — they may point to the whole abdomen
Diarrhea more common in children than adults with appendicitis
Higher fever (38.5-40°C) more common in pediatric appendicitis
Perforation rate very high in young children (40-70% in under-5s) — inability to describe symptoms causes delay
Child may walk bent forward or to the right (antalgic posture), refuse to jump, or be unwilling to stand straight
Crying, irritability, or inconsolable behaviour in infants without clear cause — consider appendicitis
Vomiting may precede pain in children (unlike adults) making diagnosis harder
Palpation of abdomen is difficult — child tenses with crying; examine gently; knee-chest position may relax abdomen
symptoms_in_elderly: Atypical presentation very common in elderly — classic pain migration present in only 20-30%
Pain may be mild, vague, or entirely absent despite advanced appendicitis
Fever may be absent or very low even in perforation (blunted immune response)
WBC may be normal or minimally elevated despite perforation
First presentation may be generalized peritonitis, septic shock, or right iliac fossa mass
High perforation rate (50-70%) due to delayed diagnosis and atypical presentation
Differential diagnosis broader (cecal cancer, diverticulitis, mesenteric ischemia) — CT essential
symptoms_in_pregnancy: Appendix displaced upward and laterally as uterus enlarges — pain may be in right upper quadrant (RUQ) or right flank rather than classic RLQ in second and third trimester
Nausea and vomiting may be attributed to pregnancy (morning sickness) causing diagnostic delay
Abdominal tenderness may be less pronounced as the gravid uterus separates the parietal peritoneum from the appendix
WBC is normally elevated in pregnancy (12,000-14,000/µL) — may mask leukocytosis of appendicitis
Perforation rate higher (43%) due to diagnostic delay
Fetal and maternal mortality significantly increased with perforation

physical_examination_signs.mcburneys_sign: Point tenderness at McBurney's point (1/3 distance from ASIS to umbilicus) — most reliable sign
physical_examination_signs.rovings_sign: Pressure on left lower quadrant causes pain in right lower quadrant — indicates peritoneal irritation; positive in appendicitis
physical_examination_signs.psoas_sign: Pain on extension of right hip (stretching iliopsoas muscle) — positive when retrocecal appendix lies against psoas muscle
physical_examination_signs.obturator_sign: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip — positive when pelvic appendix lies adjacent to obturator internus muscle
physical_examination_signs.blumbergs_sign_rebound: Pain on sudden release of deep palpation pressure — indicates peritoneal irritation
physical_examination_signs.dunphys_sign: Increased RLQ pain on coughing — peritoneal irritation sign
physical_examination_signs.ten_horn_sign: Pain on gentle traction of right testis — suggests appendiceal involvement near right spermatic cord

medical_history: Detailed pain history: onset, location, character, radiation, timing of migration from periumbilical to RLQ
Gastrointestinal symptoms: anorexia (very important), nausea, vomiting, bowel changes, last bowel movement
Urinary symptoms: dysuria, frequency (rule out UTI; pelvic appendix can cause urinary symptoms)
Fever — time of onset relative to pain
Menstrual history in women — LMP (last menstrual period); risk of ectopic pregnancy, ovarian pathology
Previous abdominal surgeries — adhesions, prior appendectomy (raises possibility of stump appendicitis)
Dietary history and recent travel (parasites in endemic areas)
Family history of appendicitis, IBD, or colorectal cancer
Medication history — immunosuppressants may mask presentation; NSAIDs may partially treat pain masking severity
physical_examination: General appearance: degree of illness, posture (antalgia — bent to right), ability to walk (limp or reluctance to move)
Vital signs: temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation
Abdominal inspection: distension, visible peristalsis, abdominal wall movement with respiration (peritonitis reduces movement)
Auscultation: bowel sounds (reduced or absent in peritonitis; may be increased in early obstruction)
Percussion: tenderness on percussion at RLQ (McBurney's point); shifting dullness if peritoneal fluid
Palpation: starting away from RLQ; McBurney's point tenderness; guarding (voluntary vs involuntary); rigidity (board-like in peritonitis); Rovsing's sign; rebound tenderness
Special signs: Psoas sign (right hip extension); Obturator sign (hip internal rotation); Dunphy's sign (cough)
Rectal examination: right-sided tenderness on digital rectal exam (pelvic appendix)
Pelvic examination in women: cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness (PID vs appendicitis)

clinical_scoring_systems.components: M-Migration of pain to RLQ (1), A-Anorexia (1), N-Nausea/vomiting (1), T-Tenderness RLQ (2), R-Rebound tenderness (1), E-Elevated temperature >37.3°C (1), L-Leukocytosis >10,000/µL (2), S-Shift to left/neutrophilia (1) — Maximum 10 points
clinical_scoring_systems.interpretation: Score 1-4: Appendicitis unlikely (observe); Score 5-6: Equivocal (CT scan); Score 7-10: High probability (surgery or CT confirmation)
clinical_scoring_systems.authority: Widely used validated score; sensitivity ~96%, specificity ~75% for score ≥7

clinical_scoring_systems.components: Vomiting (1), RLQ tenderness (1-2), rebound tenderness (1-3), WBC count (1-2), proportion neutrophils (1-2), CRP (1-2) — Maximum 12 points
clinical_scoring_systems.interpretation: Score ≤4: Low probability; 5-8: Indeterminate (imaging); ≥9: High probability (surgery)

clinical_scoring_systems.components: CRP, WBC, neutrophilia, pain migration, rebound/guarding, gender
clinical_scoring_systems.authority: Validated in Finnish population; designed for adults

diagnostic_tests.description: Leukocytosis (elevated WBC) with neutrophilia (left shift) is the most common and important laboratory finding in appendicitis. WBC 10,000-18,000/µL typical in uncomplicated; >18,000/µL suggests gangrenous or perforated appendicitis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirms systemic inflammatory response; helps assess severity and probability of appendicitis
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: WBC: Normal 4,500-11,000/µL; Appendicitis: 10,000-20,000/µL; Perforation: >18,000/µL; Neutrophil percentage >75% (neutrophilia) — 'left shift'

diagnostic_tests.description: Acute phase protein rising within 6-12 hours of inflammation onset. Highly elevated CRP combined with high WBC strongly suggests appendicitis or complicated/perforated appendicitis. CRP may be normal in very early appendicitis (<6 hours).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess severity of inflammation; combined with WBC increases diagnostic accuracy; component of AIR score
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal: <5 mg/L; Appendicitis: typically >10 mg/L; Perforation: often >50-100 mg/L

diagnostic_tests.description: Hyperbilirubinemia (elevated bilirubin) has been identified as a marker of appendiceal perforation or gangrene. Bilirubin >1.0 mg/dL combined with WBC and CRP improves diagnostic accuracy for complicated appendicitis.
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Bilirubin >1.0 mg/dL in context of acute appendicitis symptoms may suggest perforation or gangrene

diagnostic_tests.description: Elevated serum lactate (>2 mmol/L) indicates tissue hypoperfusion or sepsis. Essential in patients with suspected perforated appendicitis and septic shock.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess for sepsis and tissue hypoperfusion in complicated appendicitis; guides resuscitation
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal: <2 mmol/L; Lactate >2 mmol/L: sepsis; >4 mmol/L: septic shock

diagnostic_tests.description: Essential test in all patients with acute abdominal pain. Used to exclude urinary tract infection (UTI), kidney stones (hematuria), and ureteric colic (which can mimic appendicitis). Note: mild pyuria or hematuria (5-10 WBCs/hpf) can occur with appendicitis from ureteral proximity — does NOT exclude appendicitis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude UTI, renal colic, and other urinary causes of RLQ pain
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Significant pyuria (>20 WBCs/hpf) or positive nitrites suggests UTI; microscopic hematuria alone does not exclude appendicitis

diagnostic_tests.description: MANDATORY in all women of childbearing age (12-50 years) presenting with acute abdominal pain. Ectopic pregnancy (ruptured or unruptured) is a life-threatening emergency that can exactly mimic appendicitis. Serum beta-hCG is more sensitive than urine hCG for early pregnancy.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude ectopic pregnancy — surgical emergency; changes management completely
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Any positive beta-hCG in a woman with acute abdominal pain requires urgent gynecological assessment and pelvic ultrasound to exclude ectopic pregnancy

diagnostic_tests.description: First-line imaging for suspected appendicitis, especially in children, pregnant women, and young women (to assess ovaries). A non-compressible appendix >6mm in diameter with periappendiceal free fluid confirms appendicitis. Sensitivity limited by bowel gas, obesity, and operator experience.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: First-line imaging; avoids radiation; assess ovaries in women; confirm diagnosis in straightforward cases
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Appendiceal diameter >6mm (non-compressible) = appendicitis; target sign (concentric rings) on cross-section; free fluid in RLQ
diagnostic_tests.limitations: Sensitivity 75-90% (operator-dependent); cannot visualize appendix in 20-30% of adults; reduced by obesity and bowel gas

diagnostic_tests.test_name: CT Scan Abdomen and Pelvis with IV Contrast
diagnostic_tests.description: Gold standard imaging for appendicitis in adults. Highest sensitivity and specificity. Clearly shows appendiceal inflammation, diameter, fecaliths, perforation, abscess, free air, and alternative diagnoses. Identifies complications (peritonitis extent) and guides surgical planning.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Gold standard diagnosis; identifies complications; guides management; reveals alternative diagnoses
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Appendiceal diameter >7mm; periappendiceal fat stranding; appendicolith; free air = perforation; periappendiceal fluid/abscess
diagnostic_tests.radiation: Uses ionising radiation — consider alternatives in young women and children; CT graded low risk

diagnostic_tests.description: Preferred imaging in pregnant women (avoids fetal radiation), children, and young women when ultrasound is inconclusive. Excellent soft tissue contrast. No ionising radiation. Shows appendiceal inflammation and surrounding structures.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Preferred in pregnancy (no radiation); children; young women; when CT inconclusive or contraindicated
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: T2-bright appendix >7mm; periappendiceal edema and fluid; MRI sensitivity ~95% for appendicitis
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Less available than CT; longer scan time; difficult in agitated or uncooperative patients

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Plain Abdominal X-Ray (Erect and Supine AXR)
diagnostic_tests.description: Limited diagnostic value for appendicitis alone. Used to exclude bowel obstruction (dilated loops, air-fluid levels), perforation (free gas under diaphragm on erect CXR/AXR), and foreign bodies. A calcified fecalith in the RLQ (5-15% of cases) is suggestive of appendicitis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude free air (perforation), bowel obstruction; detect calcified appendicolith (minority of cases)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Free air under diaphragm on erect CXR = perforation (surgical emergency); calcified RLQ shadow = possible appendicolith
diagnostic_tests.note: Normal AXR does NOT exclude appendicitis; CT or US required for confirmation

diagnostic_tests.description: When clinical diagnosis remains uncertain after imaging, diagnostic laparoscopy allows direct visualization of the appendix and pelvic organs. In women of childbearing age, laparoscopy is particularly valuable to assess for ovarian pathology, PID, and ectopic pregnancy simultaneously. Can proceed to therapeutic appendectomy immediately.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Definitive diagnosis when clinical and imaging evaluation inconclusive; particularly in women; simultaneous diagnosis and treatment
diagnostic_tests.advantage: Converts to therapeutic appendectomy immediately; assesses pelvic organs; negative exploration rate reduced to <5%

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Electrolytes, Renal Function, LFTs, and Clotting Studies
diagnostic_tests.description: Pre-operative workup for all patients undergoing appendectomy. Electrolytes assess dehydration (hyponatremia, hypokalemia) and guide IV fluid management. Renal function for dose adjustment. LFTs detect liver pathology (biliary causes). Clotting for surgical risk assessment.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Pre-operative assessment; guide fluid resuscitation; exclude alternative diagnoses (biliary colic, pancreatitis)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Amylase/lipase elevation excludes pancreatitis; LFT elevation suggests biliary pathology

medicines.note: Appendicitis is primarily a surgical condition — appendectomy is the definitive treatment. Medications are used for pain control, antibiotic prophylaxis/treatment, symptom management, and non-operative management in selected cases. All medications must be prescribed by a licensed physician or surgeon. Self-medication of abdominal pain is dangerous — it may mask symptoms and delay diagnosis.

categories.purpose: Single prophylactic dose given 30-60 minutes before appendectomy incision for uncomplicated appendicitis. Therapeutic (multi-dose) course for complicated (gangrenous/perforated) appendicitis continuing post-operatively.
categories.note: Choice of antibiotics covers gram-negative enteric organisms (E. coli, Klebsiella) and anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis) — the predominant organisms in appendicitis.

medicines.name: Cefazolin + Metronidazole
medicines.dosage: Cefazolin: 1-2g IV single prophylactic dose (30-60 min pre-op); Metronidazole: 500mg IV (or 1g suppository pre-op); For complicated: continue every 8 hours for 3-5 days
medicines.use_case: Standard prophylactic combination for uncomplicated appendicitis; post-op coverage for uncomplicated
medicines.mechanism: Cefazolin: 1st generation cephalosporin — covers gram-positive and gram-negative aerobes; Metronidazole: nitroimidazole — covers anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis)
side_effects: Cefazolin: hypersensitivity (if penicillin allergy — use gentamicin instead)
Metronidazole: metallic taste, nausea, headache, peripheral neuropathy (prolonged use)

medicines.name: Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole
medicines.dosage: Ceftriaxone: 1-2g IV once daily; Metronidazole: 500mg IV every 8 hours or 1g every 12 hours
medicines.use_case: Prophylaxis and treatment for complicated appendicitis; once-daily ceftriaxone simplifies dosing; widely used regimen globally
medicines.mechanism: Ceftriaxone: 3rd generation cephalosporin — excellent gram-negative coverage

medicines.name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo)
medicines.dosage: 4.5g (4g piperacillin + 0.5g tazobactam) IV every 8 hours (extended infusion over 4 hours preferred for serious infections)
medicines.use_case: First-line for perforated appendicitis with generalized peritonitis; covers gram-positive, gram-negative (including Pseudomonas), and anaerobes; broad spectrum
medicines.mechanism: Ureidopenicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor — broadest beta-lactam coverage; Pseudomonas active

medicines.name: Imipenem-Cilastatin (Imipenem)
medicines.dosage: 500mg IV every 6 hours or 1g every 8 hours
medicines.use_case: Severe perforated appendicitis with generalized sepsis/peritonitis; resistant organisms; hospital-acquired infections; second-line carbapenem
medicines.mechanism: Carbapenem — ultra-broad spectrum including resistant gram-negatives and anaerobes
side_effects: Seizures (at high doses or renal impairment)

medicines.name: Gentamicin + Metronidazole + Amoxicillin
medicines.dosage: Gentamicin: 5-7 mg/kg IV once daily (weight-based); Metronidazole: 500 mg every 8h; Amoxicillin: 500mg-1g every 8h
medicines.use_case: Alternative for penicillin-allergic patients; triple antibiotic therapy providing full peritoneal coverage
side_effects: Nephrotoxicity (gentamicin — monitor renal function, avoid in renal impairment)
medicines.monitoring: Serum gentamicin trough levels; daily renal function; avoid with other nephrotoxins

categories.category_name: Oral Antibiotics for Non-Operative Management and Step-Down Therapy
categories.purpose: Non-operative (antibiotic-only) management of uncomplicated appendicitis has emerged as a safe option for carefully selected patients. Also used as oral step-down after IV antibiotics for complicated appendicitis hospital discharge.
categories.note: Non-operative management is an option for uncomplicated appendicitis (no fecalith, no perforation, no gangrene on CT) in adults. Success rate ~70-80% at 1 year; 20-30% require appendectomy within 1 year. Requires informed patient consent.

medicines.name: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (Co-Amoxiclav)
medicines.dosage: 875mg/125mg twice daily orally for 7-10 days (non-operative management step-down); 1.2g IV every 8 hours (hospitalized)
medicines.use_case: Oral non-operative management of uncomplicated appendicitis; step-down from IV antibiotics after complicated appendicitis
medicines.mechanism: Aminopenicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor — covers gram-positives, gram-negatives, and anaerobes
side_effects: GI upset and diarrhea (most common — take with food)
Liver dysfunction (cholestatic jaundice — more with co-amoxiclav than amoxicillin alone)

medicines.name: Ciprofloxacin + Metronidazole
medicines.dosage: Ciprofloxacin: 500mg twice daily; Metronidazole: 400-500mg three times daily; for 7-10 days
medicines.use_case: Non-operative management of uncomplicated appendicitis; penicillin allergy; oral step-down after IV therapy
side_effects: Ciprofloxacin: tendinopathy/tendon rupture (avoid in elderly, on steroids)
medicines.warning: Ciprofloxacin — avoid in children and adolescents under 18 (cartilage effects); avoid in pregnant women; FDA black box warning for serious musculoskeletal and CNS adverse effects

categories.purpose: Adequate pain relief is ESSENTIAL and does NOT mask the diagnosis — evidence-based studies confirm that opioid analgesia in suspected appendicitis does not impair diagnostic accuracy and significantly improves patient comfort. Withholding analgesics is unnecessary and cruel.
categories.note: American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) and ACEP guidelines recommend early analgesia in acute abdominal pain.

medicines.name: Morphine Sulfate
medicines.dosage: 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV every 4-6 hours titrated to pain; typical adult: 2-5 mg IV every 4-6 hours; PCA (patient-controlled analgesia) post-op
medicines.use_case: Gold standard opioid analgesic for acute severe abdominal pain in suspected/confirmed appendicitis; post-operative pain management
medicines.monitoring: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, sedation score; naloxone available as reversal agent

medicines.name: Paracetamol / Acetaminophen (IV)
medicines.dosage: 1000mg IV every 6 hours (adults ≥50kg); 15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours (children); oral 1g every 6h if tolerated
medicines.use_case: First-line non-opioid analgesic; multimodal analgesia; reduces opioid requirements post-operatively; safe in all ages
side_effects: Minimal at therapeutic doses; hepatotoxicity with overdose
medicines.note: Part of multimodal analgesia protocol — scheduled paracetamol reduces opioid requirements by 20-30%

medicines.name: Ketorolac (IV NSAID)
medicines.dosage: 15-30 mg IV/IM every 6 hours; maximum 120 mg/day; limit to 5 days
medicines.use_case: Potent IV NSAID for acute surgical pain; reduces post-operative opioid requirement; anti-inflammatory
side_effects: Platelet inhibition (avoid >5 days; avoid peri-operatively if bleeding risk)

medicines.name: Fentanyl
medicines.dosage: 0.5-1 mcg/kg IV slow push (titrate); typical adult: 25-100 mcg IV
medicines.use_case: Short-acting opioid for acute pain in ED; useful in hemodynamically unstable patients; rapid onset
medicines.note: Preferred over morphine in hemodynamic instability (less hypotensive effect)

medicines.name: Tramadol
medicines.dosage: 50-100 mg slow IV or IM every 6-8 hours; max 400 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Moderate post-operative pain; step-down from IV morphine; useful when opioid side effects problematic

medicines.name: Diclofenac Suppository / Tablet
medicines.dosage: 50-100mg rectal suppository every 12-18 hours (post-operative); 50mg oral three times daily
medicines.use_case: Post-operative analgesia when oral route established; anti-inflammatory reducing post-surgical swelling
medicines.note: Suppository useful when patient is nauseated and cannot tolerate oral medications

categories.purpose: Control nausea and vomiting — common in appendicitis and post-operatively from general anaesthesia.

medicines.name: Ondansetron
medicines.form: IV Injection, Oral tablet, Oral dissolving tablet
medicines.dosage: 4-8mg IV/orally every 8-12 hours; single 8mg IV dose for PONV (post-op nausea and vomiting)
medicines.use_case: First-line antiemetic for acute appendicitis nausea; post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV) prevention and treatment
medicines.mechanism: Selective 5-HT3 (serotonin) receptor antagonist; blocks nausea signals in CTZ and peripherally

medicines.name: Metoclopramide
medicines.dosage: 10mg IV/IM/orally every 8 hours
medicines.use_case: Antiemetic and prokinetic; enhances gastric emptying; useful pre-operatively and post-operatively
side_effects: Extrapyramidal effects (acute dystonia — especially in young patients; treat with procyclidine)

medicines.name: Promethazine
medicines.dosage: 25mg IM/IV slowly every 6-8 hours; 10-25mg orally
medicines.use_case: Antiemetic and antihistamine; useful when ondansetron unavailable
side_effects: Avoid IV bolus — tissue necrosis risk if extravasated

categories.purpose: Patients with appendicitis — especially perforated — are dehydrated from reduced oral intake, vomiting, fever, and peritoneal fluid losses. IV fluid resuscitation is essential pre-operatively and peri-operatively.

medicines.name: Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl) / Hartmann's Solution (Lactated Ringer's)
medicines.dosage: 1-2L IV bolus over 30-60 minutes for initial resuscitation of dehydrated/septic patient; then maintenance 1-2 mL/kg/hour; goal-directed: target MAP >65 mmHg, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/hour
medicines.use_case: IV fluid resuscitation for dehydration, pre-operative preparation, and sepsis management in perforated appendicitis
side_effects: Hyperchloremic acidosis (large volume normal saline — Hartmann's preferred to avoid this)
medicines.note: Hartmann's (lactated Ringer's) is the preferred balanced crystalloid for surgical patients — less acidosis than normal saline

medicines.name: 5% Dextrose (D5W) / Dextrose-Saline
medicines.dosage: Post-operatively when oral intake restricted; maintenance 1.5-2 mL/kg/hour; add potassium if ileus
medicines.use_case: Post-operative maintenance fluid when patient NPO (nil per oral); provides calories and hydration
side_effects: Hyponatremia (with 5% dextrose — avoid as resuscitation fluid)

categories.purpose: Appendectomy (surgical removal of the appendix) is the definitive and standard treatment for acute appendicitis. Available as laparoscopic (minimally invasive, preferred) or open technique.
categories.note: Appendectomy is the most commonly performed emergency abdominal surgery worldwide. All surgeries require general anaesthesia.

medicines.name: Laparoscopic Appendectomy
medicines.description: Three small incisions (5-12mm ports) allow camera and instruments entry. Appendix visualized, mesoappendix ligated, appendix stapled/ligated and removed. Benefits: less pain, faster recovery, shorter hospital stay, better cosmesis, lower wound infection rate, ability to inspect entire abdomen.
medicines.technique: 3 ports: umbilical (camera, 10-12mm), suprapubic (5mm), RLQ or LLQ (5mm); appendix stapled with endostapler and retrieved via umbilical port
advantages: Preferred over open for all patient types
contraindications_relative: Severe peritonitis where laparotomy gives better access

medicines.name: Open Appendectomy
medicines.description: Gridiron (McBurney's) or Lanz incision in RLQ over McBurney's point. Appendix identified, mesoappendix ligated, appendix removed, stump ligated or buried. Used when laparoscopy not available or when conversion from laparoscopy necessary.
medicines.technique: RLQ incision (Gridiron incision — muscle-splitting through McBurney's point, or Lanz — transverse skin crease incision); identifies cecum → follows to appendix; appendix removed; peritoneal washout for perforation
medicines.use_case: When laparoscopic equipment unavailable; conversion from failed laparoscopic; perforation with extensive soiling; pregnancy (some surgeons prefer open); hemodynamic instability
advantages: Allows thorough peritoneal washout in generalized peritonitis

medicines.name: Image-Guided Percutaneous Drainage
medicines.description: Ultrasound or CT-guided insertion of a drainage catheter into a periappendiceal abscess. Evacuates pus, allows IV antibiotics to work, avoids emergency surgery in a sick patient. Followed by interval appendectomy 6-8 weeks later.
medicines.use_case: Appendiceal abscess or phlegmon with well-defined collection; patient too unwell for emergency surgery; bridge to interval appendectomy
advantages: Avoids emergency surgery in complicated cases
Allows patient optimization before interval operation
medicines.note: Requires experienced interventional radiology team; may not be available at all centers

categories.purpose: Medications and care protocols to optimize post-operative recovery, prevent complications, and promote wound healing.

medicines.name: Prophylactic Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH)
medicines.dosage: Enoxaparin: 40mg SC once daily (prophylaxis); start 6-12 hours post-operatively; continue until mobile
medicines.use_case: Post-operative DVT and pulmonary embolism prophylaxis; abdominal surgery increases VTE risk significantly

medicines.name: Proton Pump Inhibitor (Omeprazole / Pantoprazole)
medicines.dosage: 40mg IV/orally once or twice daily
medicines.use_case: Stress ulcer prophylaxis in critically ill perforated appendicitis patients; gastric protection during NSAID use

medicines.name: Stool Softeners / Laxatives
medicines.dosage: Lactulose: 15-30mL twice daily; Bisacodyl: 5-10mg orally at night
medicines.use_case: Post-operative constipation — common from opioids, reduced mobility, dietary changes; prevent straining at stool (reduces wound dehiscence risk)

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Dietary management in appendicitis follows three distinct phases: (1) Pre-operative phase — NPO (nothing by mouth) until surgery; (2) Immediate post-operative phase (24-72 hours) — graduated return to oral intake; (3) Long-term recovery phase — nutritious, high-fibre diet to support healing and promote bowel health. There is no specific diet that prevents appendicitis, but a high-fibre diet is associated with lower risk of fecalith formation and appendicitis.

phase_1_pre_operative.instruction: NPO (Nil Per Os — Nothing By Mouth)
phase_1_pre_operative.details: Once appendicitis is suspected or confirmed, patient must not eat or drink anything orally until after surgery. IV fluids are administered to maintain hydration. Even water by mouth is withheld to ensure empty stomach for safe general anaesthesia (aspiration prevention — Mendelson's syndrome).
phase_1_pre_operative.duration: From time of diagnosis until at least 2-4 hours post-operatively or until bowel sounds return

foods: Sips of water when fully awake and gag reflex returned
step_1.instructions: Start with 30-60 mL water every 30 minutes; advance if no vomiting; listen for returning bowel sounds

foods: Clear liquids: water, weak tea, clear broth, apple juice (no pulp)
step_2.instructions: Take small sips; stop and rest if nausea occurs; avoid carbonated drinks (gas causes discomfort in laparoscopic patients from CO2 insufflation)

foods: Full liquid diet: soups (strained), yogurt, ice cream (limited), smoothies
step_3.instructions: Advance if tolerating clear liquids; continue only if no nausea, vomiting, or abdominal distension

foods: Soft diet: boiled rice, khichdi (rice and lentil porridge), oatmeal, scrambled eggs, mashed potatoes, steamed fish
step_4.instructions: Avoid fibrous, raw, spicy, or fried foods until surgical site is healed; small frequent meals

recommended_foods.category: High-Fibre Foods (Long-term recovery and prevention of future GI issues)

items.food: Whole grains: Brown rice, Oats, Whole wheat bread, Quinoa, Barley
items.benefit: Dietary fibre reduces fecalith formation and constipation — primary cause of appendiceal obstruction. High-fibre diet associated with lower appendicitis incidence in epidemiological studies. Supports healthy bowel flora and gut motility.

items.food: Fruits with skin: Apples, Pears, Berries, Guava, Papaya
items.benefit: Soluble and insoluble fibre; antioxidants support wound healing; Vitamin C promotes collagen synthesis for scar formation; natural anti-inflammatory

items.food: Vegetables: Broccoli, Carrots, Spinach, Sweet potatoes, Beetroot
items.benefit: Fibre, vitamins, antioxidants; support gut microbiome recovery after antibiotics; Vitamin A and C for wound healing
items.frequency: Daily; well-cooked initially (week 1-2); raw from week 3+

items.food: Legumes: Lentils, Chickpeas, Dal, Kidney beans
items.benefit: High fibre (5-8g per serving); plant protein for tissue repair; prebiotic effect supports gut bacteria recovery after perioperative antibiotics
Complete protein — all essential amino acids for tissue repair and immune recovery; easily digestible; Vitamin D, B12, and zinc support wound healing

items.food: Chicken broth and lean boiled chicken
items.benefit: Easily digestible protein; collagen from bone broth supports gut mucosal healing; electrolytes from broth replace losses from fever and vomiting; glycine supports liver detoxification post-anaesthesia

items.food: Fish (steamed or boiled): Salmon, Tuna, Pomfret, Rohu
items.benefit: Lean high-quality protein; omega-3 anti-inflammatory fatty acids promote wound healing and reduce surgical inflammation; Vitamin D

items.food: Low-fat dairy: Yogurt, Curd, Paneer, Skimmed milk
items.benefit: Protein for tissue repair; calcium for bone health; yogurt — probiotics essential to restore gut microbiome after broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (reduces antibiotic-associated diarrhea, C. difficile risk)
items.frequency: Daily; yogurt especially important during and after antibiotic course

items.benefit: Excellent post-surgical recovery food in Indian context: easy to digest, protein-rich, warm, hydrating, gut-soothing, anti-inflammatory spices (turmeric, cumin)
items.frequency: Daily in first 2 weeks of recovery

items.food: Plain yogurt / Curd with live cultures
items.benefit: CRITICAL after antibiotic therapy: restores Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium gut flora disrupted by perioperative broad-spectrum antibiotics; prevents antibiotic-associated diarrhea and Clostridioides difficile colitis; improves gut barrier function
items.frequency: Daily during antibiotic course and 2-4 weeks after completion

items.benefit: Multiple Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains; supports gut mucosal healing post-surgery; anti-inflammatory

items.food: Fermented foods: Idli, Dosa (fermented rice/dal), Kanji (rice water)
items.benefit: Natural probiotics from fermentation; easily digestible; traditional Indian foods with gut-healing properties; light on surgical digestive system

Adequate hydration prevents constipation (reduces fecalith formation); supports kidney function (especially important while on antibiotics); prevents dehydration from fever-related losses; promotes wound healing
items.frequency: 8-10 glasses (2-2.5 liters) daily from day 1 post-surgery

items.benefit: Electrolyte replacement (sodium, potassium, glucose) for patients dehydrated from vomiting and reduced intake pre-surgery

items.food: Warm herbal teas: Ginger tea, Chamomile, Peppermint
items.benefit: Ginger: anti-nausea, anti-inflammatory; Chamomile: calms gut spasms; Peppermint: relieves abdominal gas and bloating (common post-laparoscopy from CO2 gas)
items.frequency: 1-3 cups daily post-surgery for nausea and gas relief

items.benefit: Hydration, electrolytes, trace minerals; easily absorbed; provides warmth and comfort; traditional recovery food
items.frequency: Multiple times daily in first 3-5 days post-surgery

recommended_foods.category: Vitamins and Minerals for Wound Healing

items.food: Vitamin C-rich foods: Amla, Oranges, Guava, Lemon, Bell peppers
items.benefit: Essential for collagen synthesis — the primary protein of wound healing and scar formation; antioxidant reduces surgical oxidative stress; supports immune function post-surgery

items.food: Zinc-rich foods: Pumpkin seeds, Chickpeas, Lentils, Lean meat
items.benefit: Zinc is essential for wound healing (cell proliferation, protein synthesis, immune function); deficiency impairs healing and increases infection risk

items.food: Vitamin A-rich foods: Sweet potato, Carrots, Spinach, Pumpkin
items.benefit: Vitamin A supports epithelial cell regeneration and mucosal healing; important for gut mucosal recovery after peritonitis

foods_to_avoid.reason: Irritate healing GI tract; increase gut motility causing discomfort at surgical site; may trigger nausea post-operatively; avoid for at least 2-4 weeks post-surgery
foods_to_avoid.duration: Avoid for 2-4 weeks post-operatively; reintroduce gradually

foods_to_avoid.reason: High-fat foods are difficult to digest post-surgery as bile secretion and gut motility are temporarily impaired; delay GI recovery; cause nausea, bloating, and diarrhea

After laparoscopic appendectomy, residual CO2 gas from pneumoperitoneum causes shoulder tip pain and abdominal distension. Carbonated drinks add to this gas discomfort significantly. Bloating and distension worsen post-operative discomfort.
foods_to_avoid.duration: Avoid for at least 1-2 weeks post-laparoscopy

foods_to_avoid.reason: Alcohol delays wound healing (impairs collagen synthesis), suppresses immune function (increases infection risk), interacts with post-operative analgesics and antibiotics (severe reaction with metronidazole — causes flushing, vomiting, hypotension), and stresses the liver recovering from anaesthesia
foods_to_avoid.duration: Avoid completely for at least 4-6 weeks post-surgery; completely contraindicated with metronidazole

foods_to_avoid.food: Raw vegetables and high-fibre foods (in the first 2 weeks)
foods_to_avoid.reason: In the immediate post-operative period, the gut needs time to recover normal motility. High-fibre raw vegetables and whole grains can be difficult to digest and may cause excessive gas, bloating, and diarrhea before bowel function normalizes.
examples: Cruciferous vegetables (cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower — gas-forming) in first week
foods_to_avoid.duration: Avoid in first 7-10 days; reintroduce gradually from week 2

foods_to_avoid.reason: Low nutritional value; contain preservatives and additives that may irritate healing gut; lack protein and micronutrients needed for wound healing; promote constipation; contraindicated in the recovery period

foods_to_avoid.food: Dairy in large amounts (if antibiotic-associated diarrhea develops)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce lactase-producing gut bacteria; temporary lactose intolerance may develop during and after antibiotic course. Switch to yogurt (lactase-producing bacteria) or lactose-free dairy temporarily.
foods_to_avoid.nuance: Plain yogurt is recommended (probiotics); small amounts of lactose-free dairy acceptable; avoid if diarrhea develops

sample_meal_plan.note: This post-appendectomy recovery meal plan guides gradual dietary advancement. Progress depends on individual recovery — follow your surgeon's specific instructions. This plan assumes uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy.
sample_meal_plan.day_0_to_1_post_op: NPO (pre-op) → ice chips → sips of water → clear liquids (water, weak tea, clear broth) as tolerated
sample_meal_plan.day_2_post_op: Clear liquids: water, clear vegetable broth, strained apple juice, weak tea with honey + oral rehydration solution if dehydrated
sample_meal_plan.day_3_post_op: Full liquids: strained dal soup, rice water (kanji), yogurt, banana smoothie (diluted), warm ginger tea
sample_meal_plan.day_4_to_5_post_op: Soft diet: Moong dal khichdi (soft rice and lentil porridge) + steamed carrot + 1 boiled egg + 1 cup plain curd
sample_meal_plan.week_2: Light diet: Soft boiled rice with dal + steamed fish or boiled chicken + steamed vegetables + curd + fresh fruits (peeled) + 8 glasses water
sample_meal_plan.week_3_to_4: Normal diet gradually resumed: Whole grains (roti, brown rice) + cooked vegetables + protein (eggs, fish, chicken, legumes) + fresh fruits + probiotic yogurt + ensure adequate fibre (25-30g daily) to prevent constipation
sample_meal_plan.long_term: High-fibre Mediterranean-style diet: variety of fruits and vegetables, whole grains, legumes, lean proteins, olive oil, adequate hydration

special_dietary_notes: Constipation is the most common post-operative dietary complication — adequate fibre (25-30g/day when fully recovered) and hydration (2-2.5L/day) are essential to prevent straining at stool (risks wound dehiscence)
Probiotics (yogurt, kefir) during and 4 weeks after antibiotic course significantly reduce risk of Clostridioides difficile colitis (antibiotic-associated diarrhea) — provide daily
Protein intake targets: 1.2-1.5 g/kg body weight daily for optimal wound healing; nutritional support important in malnourished patients
Vitamin C supplementation (500mg daily for 4-6 weeks) may support wound collagen synthesis, especially in patients with poor nutritional status pre-operatively
Zinc supplementation (15-25mg daily for 4-6 weeks) supports wound healing if dietary intake inadequate

Patients who underwent perforated appendicitis with prolonged ileus may require nasogastric tube feeding or parenteral nutrition (TPN) if unable to eat for >5-7 days — nutritional support specialist input essential
Resume normal diet gradually — every patient's recovery is different; pain, nausea, and bowel function guide dietary progression

laparoscopic_appendectomy.hospital_stay: 1-2 days for uncomplicated; 3-7 days for complicated/perforated
laparoscopic_appendectomy.day_1_to_3: Rest; short walks around the ward/home every 1-2 hours to prevent DVT; no heavy lifting; avoid driving
laparoscopic_appendectomy.week_1_to_2: Light activities (walking, gentle household tasks); no lifting >5kg; no driving while on opioids; wound care (keep incisions dry for 48 hours, then gentle cleaning)
laparoscopic_appendectomy.week_2_to_4: Gradually increase activity; can return to desk/office work at 1-2 weeks if pain controlled; no strenuous activity or gym
laparoscopic_appendectomy.week_4_to_6: Resume most normal activities; gym and sports at 4-6 weeks with clearance from surgeon
laparoscopic_appendectomy.return_to_work: Sedentary jobs: 1-2 weeks; manual/physical jobs: 3-6 weeks

open_appendectomy.hospital_stay: 2-4 days uncomplicated; 5-10 days for perforated with peritonitis
open_appendectomy.week_1_to_2: Rest; short indoor walks; no lifting >2kg; wound care essential (larger wound)
open_appendectomy.week_2_to_4: Gentle walking; gradual increase; avoid anything that strains abdominal muscles
open_appendectomy.week_4_to_8: Progressive return to normal; gym and manual work at 6-8 weeks

perforated_appendicitis_with_peritonitis.recovery_timeline: Full recovery 4-8 weeks; extended convalescence; physiotherapy may be required for deconditioning from prolonged illness

wound_care: Keep surgical wounds clean and dry for 48 hours post-operation
After 48 hours: gently clean wounds with clean water and mild soap; pat dry gently
Check wounds daily for signs of infection: increasing redness, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge, or opening of wound edges
Keep wounds covered with sterile dressings until advised by surgeon to leave open to air
Avoid submerging wounds in baths, swimming pools, or sea water until fully healed (usually 2-3 weeks for laparoscopic; 3-4 weeks for open)
Showers acceptable from 48-72 hours if wound covered with waterproof dressing
Dissolvable sutures (absorbable) dissolve on their own (2-4 weeks); non-dissolvable clips or sutures removed at 7-10 days
Laparoscopic port site wounds heal faster; open wound (McBurney's) takes 3-6 weeks for full skin healing
Contact surgeon immediately if wound opens (dehiscence), significant bleeding, or increasing pain at wound site
breathing_exercises: Deep breathing exercises from day 1 post-operation — prevents post-operative atelectasis (lung collapse) and pneumonia
Incentive spirometry: breathe deeply and hold for 3-5 seconds; 10 repetitions every hour while awake in hospital
Supported coughing: hold pillow firmly against abdomen during coughing to reduce wound pain and support suture line
Early mobilization (walking) is the best respiratory prevention — promotes lung expansion
dvt_prevention: Wear graduated compression stockings (TED stockings) from surgery until fully mobile
Ankle pumping exercises in bed (dorsiflexion-plantarflexion) every 30 minutes when lying down
Get out of bed and walk as soon as pain allows — usually day 1 post-operation
IV heparin (LMWH) prophylaxis subcutaneously as prescribed
Report immediately: calf pain and swelling (DVT); sudden breathlessness and chest pain (pulmonary embolism)
pain_management_at_home: Take prescribed analgesics regularly for the first 48-72 hours — do not wait for pain to become severe
Multimodal analgesia: regular paracetamol (1g every 6 hours) + ibuprofen (400mg every 8 hours with food) usually adequate for laparoscopic appendectomy
Shoulder tip pain after laparoscopic surgery is normal — from residual CO2 gas irritating the diaphragm; resolves in 24-48 hours; peppermint tea and gentle walking help
Abdominal pain at wound sites normal for 1-2 weeks; severe worsening pain not controlled by analgesics — contact surgeon
Avoid lying flat for prolonged periods — semi-recumbent position (30-45 degrees) reduces abdominal muscle tension
mental_health_and_recovery: Anxiety about recovery and complications is common — discuss concerns with surgeon at follow-up
Most patients feel significantly better within 1-2 weeks of laparoscopic appendectomy
Post-operative fatigue is normal and expected — allow adequate rest and do not rush return to work or activities
Children may have school anxiety after hospitalization — gradual return with school support; explain need for wound protection in sports/PE
Psychological impact of emergency surgery should not be underestimated — some patients experience anxiety, nightmares, or PTSD after severe perforated appendicitis; psychological support available
Support from family and friends during recovery is important — accept help with household tasks during first 2 weeks

appendicitis_monitoring_plan.note: Appendicitis monitoring has two phases: (1) Emergency monitoring — assessment in the ED/ward while awaiting surgery; (2) Post-operative monitoring — recovery tracking at home. If symptoms of appendicitis are suspected, immediate medical evaluation is mandatory.

green_zone.criteria: Pain reducing daily (2-3/10 at rest, controlled with oral analgesics); bowel sounds present; passing flatus; tolerating oral liquids/soft diet; afebrile or low-grade fever only in first 24-48 hours post-op; wound healing with no signs of infection; normal activity gradually increasing
green_zone.action: Continue recovery plan; oral analgesics as needed; progressive diet advancement; wound care; follow-up appointment at 1-2 weeks post-discharge

yellow_zone.criteria: Fever >38°C beyond 48 hours post-operation; increasing rather than decreasing abdominal pain; wound increasingly red, warm, swollen or discharging pus; unable to keep fluids down due to nausea/vomiting at home; not passing flatus or opening bowels by day 3-4 (possible ileus or obstruction); persistent diarrhea after antibiotics
yellow_zone.action: Contact surgeon or GP within 24 hours. If fever and wound redness, attend wound clinic. Blood tests (CBC, CRP) and wound swab may be required. Consider IV antibiotics for wound infection. Most post-operative complications are treatable if identified early.

red_zone.status: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Immediate Hospital Attention Required
red_zone.criteria: Any of: high fever >39°C with abdominal pain and rigidity (peritonitis); acute severe abdominal pain worse than post-operative baseline (possible internal bleeding, anastomotic leak, or bowel obstruction); signs of sepsis (tachycardia, hypotension, confusion, cold extremities); abdominal distension and inability to pass flatus (bowel obstruction from adhesions); wound completely opening (dehiscence); unexplained initial severe RLQ pain with no appendectomy yet performed — possible appendicitis
red_zone.action: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112 India; 999 UK; 911 USA) or go to nearest emergency department immediately. Do not wait. If pre-diagnosis: do NOT eat or drink anything while waiting — surgery may be needed urgently (NPO essential for anaesthesia).

complications.description: Most feared complication of untreated appendicitis. Perforation occurs in 20-30% of all cases; up to 70% in children under 5 and elderly over 70 (due to delayed diagnosis and atypical presentation). Free perforation causes generalized bacterial peritonitis with life-threatening sepsis. Even with surgery, mortality increases significantly.
complications.timing: Usually 24-72 hours from symptom onset; but highly variable
complications.prevention: Prompt diagnosis and appendectomy within 24 hours of presentation

complications.description: Localized collection of pus walled off by omentum and bowel, forming a phlegmon or frank abscess around the perforated appendix. Presents as prolonged symptoms (>5-7 days), RLQ mass, persistent fever, and high CRP/WBC. Managed with drainage and antibiotics ± interval appendectomy.
complications.management: IR-guided drainage + IV antibiotics; interval appendectomy 6-8 weeks later

complications.description: Most common post-operative complication. Open appendectomy wound infection rate 5-10%; laparoscopic <3%. Presents with redness, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge from wound, fever, and rising WBC at 5-7 days post-op. Caused by contamination during surgery (especially in perforated cases).
complications.management: Wound opening and drainage; wound swab and antibiotics; regular wound dressing changes

complications.description: Deep pelvic or abdominal abscess forming after perforated appendicitis or complicated surgery. Presents as persistent fever (>38.5°C), abdominal pain, and high CRP/WBC 5-7 days post-operation. CT-guided drainage required.
complications.management: CT scan confirmation; IR-guided percutaneous drainage; prolonged IV antibiotics

complications.description: Temporary cessation of normal peristaltic bowel activity after abdominal surgery or from peritoneal irritation. Presents as abdominal distension, no passage of flatus, inability to tolerate oral intake, and vomiting. Usually resolves within 3-5 days with conservative management.
complications.management: IV fluids; nasogastric tube if vomiting; chewing gum surprisingly evidence-based for ileus; early mobilization; prokinetics (metoclopramide); most resolves spontaneously

complications.description: Post-operative adhesions (fibrous scar bands) between bowel loops, omentum, and peritoneum can cause bowel kinking or constriction, leading to small bowel obstruction (SBO). This can occur weeks, months, or years after appendectomy — especially after perforated appendicitis. Presents with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, and absolute constipation.
complications.management: Initial conservative management (IV fluids, NGT decompression); surgical division of adhesions if not resolving or strangulation suspected

complications.description: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection — in this case from perforated appendicitis with bacterial peritonitis. Presents with fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status, high lactate, and multi-organ failure.
complications.management: ICU admission; Surviving Sepsis Campaign bundle: blood cultures THEN IV antibiotics within 1 hour; IV fluid resuscitation 30 mL/kg; vasopressors if hypotension persists; emergency surgery for source control

complications.description: Rare but dangerous — inflammation of an incompletely removed appendiceal remnant (stump >5mm left behind at appendectomy). Presents exactly like acute appendicitis but patients and clinicians may not consider appendicitis as the diagnosis (patient believes they have had their appendix removed).
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe (risks perforation as in original appendicitis)
complications.management: Laparoscopic or open re-exploration and complete stump excision

complications.description: Perforated appendicitis with pelvic peritonitis can cause adhesion formation around the fallopian tubes and ovaries, potentially impairing tubal patency and ovarian function. Associated with increased risk of ectopic pregnancy and infertility — particularly in women with right-sided tubal involvement from perforated appendicitis.
complications.management: Pelvic physiotherapy; fertility specialist assessment if difficulties conceiving; hysterosalpingography (HSG) to assess tubal patency

complications.description: Weakness at the abdominal wall incision site allowing bowel or omentum to protrude. More common after open appendectomy (especially with wound infection or dehiscence) than laparoscopic. Presents as a lump at the incision site, worsening on coughing or straining.
complications.management: Surgical hernia repair (hernioplasty with mesh); avoid heavy lifting and straining until wound fully healed to prevent

complications.complication: Right Iliac Fossa Pain Syndrome (Post-Appendectomy Syndrome)
complications.description: Persistent or recurrent RLQ pain after appendectomy (occurring in up to 10% of patients). Causes include: appendix not truly inflamed (negative appendectomy), overlooked co-existing pathology (Meckel's diverticulum, Crohn's, mesenteric adenitis, ovarian cyst), adhesional pain, or chronic pelvic pain. Requires systematic investigation.
complications.management: Further investigation (CT, colonoscopy, gynaecological evaluation); multidisciplinary team approach

key_points: Peak incidence in school-age children (10-14 years); all ages can be affected including infants

Perforation rate very high — 40-70% in children under 5; up to 100% in infants — primarily because young children cannot localize and communicate pain; atypical presentation; delay in seeking medical attention
Lymphoid hyperplasia most common cause in children (vs fecalith in adults); often triggered by viral illness
Symptoms may be non-specific in young children: poor feeding, irritability, excessive crying, vomiting, fever, refusal to walk
Rovsing's sign and Psoas sign may be difficult to elicit in crying, uncooperative children — examine gently in parent's lap
Ultrasound preferred over CT for initial imaging in children (no radiation) — though sensitivity lower; MRI second choice if ultrasound inconclusive
Use of CT in children must be judicious — radiation concern; use only when necessary and US/MRI inconclusive
Alvarado score validated in children; Paediatric Appendicitis Score (PAS) also commonly used in pediatric populations
Post-operative recovery faster in children; oral feeding can often start same day as surgery
Laparoscopic appendectomy standard in children at experienced pediatric surgery centers
Children with suspected appendicitis must be seen by paediatric surgeon urgently — do NOT observe at home if suspicion raised
Most common non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy — occurs 1:1000 pregnancies
Perforation rate in pregnancy is 43% vs 20% in non-pregnant women — due to diagnostic delay from atypical presentation and attribution of symptoms to pregnancy
Appendix displacement: by 2nd trimester the appendix migrates to RUQ (right upper quadrant) and right flank as uterus grows — pain is NOT in classic RLQ in later pregnancy
WBC normally elevated in pregnancy (up to 14,000/µL) reducing utility of leukocytosis as a diagnostic sign
Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (morning sickness) can mask appendicitis symptoms
MRI is the preferred imaging modality in pregnancy — no fetal radiation risk; high sensitivity for appendicitis
Ultrasound first but often limited by gravid uterus in later trimesters
CT scan acceptable if MRI unavailable and high clinical suspicion — benefit of diagnosis outweighs radiation risk to fetus
Laparoscopic appendectomy is safe in all trimesters with experienced surgeon and anaesthetist — fetal outcomes similar to open in 2nd trimester
Beta-hCG MANDATORY in all women of childbearing age with RLQ pain — ectopic pregnancy must be excluded
Maternal and fetal mortality significantly higher with perforated appendicitis — perforation causes premature labour, fetal distress, and pregnancy loss
Post-operative tocolysis may be required to prevent premature labour after surgery in 2nd trimester
Antibiotics: avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines in pregnancy; cefazolin + metronidazole acceptable
Less common but significantly more dangerous — mortality 4-10x higher than young adults
Perforation rate 40-70% in elderly — due to atypical presentation and delayed diagnosis
Classic features absent in 30-40% of elderly: pain migration may not occur; fever may be absent (blunted immune response); WBC may be normal despite perforation
First presentation often with localized RLQ mass (abscess), diffuse peritonitis, or unexplained sepsis
CT scan ESSENTIAL in elderly with any RLQ pain or unexplained fever and abdominal symptoms — clinical diagnosis unreliable
Must consider alternative diagnoses: cecal carcinoma obstructing appendix, sigmoid diverticulitis, mesenteric ischemia — all more common in elderly
Pre-existing comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, diabetes, CKD, anticoagulants) significantly increase surgical and anaesthetic risk
Laparoscopic appendectomy preferred in elderly when possible — reduced complication rate; faster recovery
Adequate resuscitation essential before surgery — elderly poorly tolerate hypovolemia
Post-operative recovery is slower; DVT risk higher; delirium common post-anaesthesia in elderly (POCD — post-operative cognitive dysfunction)
Close monitoring for surgical complications is essential; early re-imaging if clinical deterioration
Patients on corticosteroids, chemotherapy, TNF inhibitors, or HIV/AIDS may have masked symptoms — steroids blunt pain and fever; immunosuppression blunts leukocytosis
Atypical organisms may cause appendicitis in immunocompromised: CMV, Mycobacteria, Candida
Low threshold for CT scan in immunocompromised patients with any abdominal symptoms
Broader antibiotic coverage required peri-operatively
Withhold immunosuppressive medications peri-operatively as clinically feasible
Higher post-operative complication rate — wound healing impaired by immunosuppression and steroids

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Appendicitis is primarily caused by luminal obstruction (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia, foreign bodies) rather than a specific preventable pathogen. No vaccine exists for appendicitis prevention.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Some viral infections (adenovirus, measles, EBV) trigger lymphoid hyperplasia that can cause appendicitis. Standard childhood immunization schedule (MMR, adenovirus vaccine in military personnel) indirectly reduces this risk.

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Viral respiratory infections (influenza) can trigger lymphoid hyperplasia throughout the gut including the appendix. General health maintenance and infection prevention reduces one predisposing factor for appendiceal lymphoid hyperplasia.

Post-operative pneumonia is a significant complication after abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia. Pneumococcal vaccination provides protection against one of the most common causes of post-operative pneumonia.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Booster every 10 years; ensure up to date before elective surgery
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Standard adult immunization; important for wound infection prophylaxis given tetanus risk from any surgical wound
COVID-19 infection increases surgical risk significantly (higher post-operative pulmonary complications). Vaccination reduces severity of COVID-19 and its complications in the peri-operative setting.

when_to_see_doctor: Abdominal pain starting around the navel and gradually moving to the right lower abdomen — even mild or moderate — warrants medical evaluation within hours
Pain in the right lower abdomen lasting more than 4-6 hours, particularly with fever and nausea
Any abdominal pain with fever (>37.5°C / 99.5°F) in a previously healthy person — especially children
Loss of appetite combined with abdominal pain — anorexia is a classic early warning sign of appendicitis
Abdominal pain worse with movement, walking, or coughing — suggests peritoneal irritation
Worsening abdominal pain in a pregnant woman at any stage of pregnancy — appendicitis in pregnancy is a surgical emergency
Child with abdominal pain limping, walking bent over, or refusing to walk — possible appendicitis
Persistent nausea and vomiting with abdominal pain for more than 12-24 hours
Any right iliac fossa pain in an elderly patient — even if mild and without fever; atypical presentations common
Post-appendectomy: fever >38°C beyond 48 hours, increasing wound pain, wound discharge, or worsening abdominal pain — possible post-operative complication
Recurrent episodes of mild right lower quadrant pain — possible chronic/recurrent appendicitis requiring investigation
emergency_signs: Sudden severe abdominal pain that rapidly spreads throughout the entire abdomen — possible appendiceal perforation and generalized peritonitis
Board-like rigid abdomen with extreme tenderness on the lightest touch — signs of generalized peritonitis
High fever above 39°C (102.2°F) with abdominal pain and deteriorating general condition
Signs of septic shock: very rapid heart rate (>120 bpm), falling blood pressure, cold and clammy sweaty skin, extreme weakness or confusion
Child or infant who is inconsolable, extremely pale, floppy, or unresponsive — possible perforated appendicitis with septic shock
Severe abdominal pain in a pregnant woman at any gestation — especially with fever and shoulder tip pain (phrenic nerve irritation from peritonitis)
Sudden brief relief of severe pain followed immediately by worsening and spreading abdominal pain — classic perforation pattern
Elderly patient with unexplained severe general deterioration, confusion, low blood pressure, and abdominal discomfort — possible perforated appendicitis presenting atypically
Abdominal distension that is rapidly worsening with inability to pass gas or stool and vomiting — intestinal obstruction or severe ileus from peritonitis
Post-appendectomy: severe worsening abdominal pain, high fever, and shock — intra-abdominal abscess, anastomotic leak, or sepsis

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is appendicitis and where is the appendix?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Appendicitis is inflammation of the vermiform appendix — a small, finger-shaped pouch (typically 9cm long) attached to the cecum (start of the large intestine) in the right lower abdomen. The appendix lies in the right iliac fossa (RIF) — the lower right quadrant of the abdomen. When it becomes obstructed and inflamed, bacteria multiply causing pain, fever, and the risk of rupture.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What does appendicitis pain feel like and where is it?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Appendicitis typically begins as a dull, crampy ache around the navel (belly button) — this is visceral pain from the distended appendix. Over the next 4-24 hours, the pain moves to the right lower abdomen at McBurney's point (about 1/3 of the way from the right hip bone to the navel) — this is somatic pain as inflammation reaches the peritoneum. The pain becomes sharper and constant, worsens with movement, and is 6-9/10 in severity.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can appendicitis get better on its own?
