frequently_asked_questions.answer: Occasionally, very mild appendicitis may resolve spontaneously, but this is the exception rather than the rule and is unpredictable. Without treatment, appendicitis typically progresses to gangrene and perforation within 24-72 hours. Non-operative (antibiotic-only) management is now an evidence-based option for carefully selected uncomplicated appendicitis — with a 70-80% success rate at 1 year. However, 20-30% of patients treated with antibiotics alone eventually require surgery. Medical assessment is always mandatory — never attempt to manage suspected appendicitis at home.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is surgery always necessary for appendicitis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Traditionally yes — appendectomy has been the standard treatment for 130 years. However, evidence now supports non-operative management (antibiotics only) as a safe initial treatment for uncomplicated appendicitis (no perforation, no fecalith) in adults. Multiple large trials (APPAC, CODA) show 70-80% success at 1 year. For complicated appendicitis (gangrenous, perforated), surgery is always required. The choice between antibiotics-only and surgery should be made together by the patient and surgeon after discussing risks and benefits.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What happens if appendicitis is not treated?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Untreated appendicitis is life-threatening. The sequence without treatment: obstruction → bacterial overgrowth → gangrene (ischemic necrosis of appendix wall) → perforation → bacterial peritonitis → septic shock → multi-organ failure → death. Perforation occurs in 20-30% overall; 40-70% in children under 5 and elderly. Even treated perforated appendicitis carries significant morbidity. Any suspicion of appendicitis requires same-day medical evaluation — delay is dangerous.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between laparoscopic and open appendectomy?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Laparoscopic (keyhole) appendectomy uses 3 small incisions (5-12mm each) with a camera and instruments — the appendix is removed through a small port. Benefits: less pain, smaller scars, 1-2 day hospital stay, return to work in 1-2 weeks, lower wound infection rate. Open appendectomy uses a single larger incision (5-7cm) in the right lower abdomen (McBurney's incision). Required when laparoscopy is not feasible (extensive adhesions, severe peritonitis), or when conversion is needed from failed laparoscopic approach. Hospital stay 2-4 days; return to work 2-4 weeks. Laparoscopic is preferred for most patients.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What should I not eat or do when appendicitis is suspected?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: If appendicitis is suspected: DO NOT eat, drink anything (including water), or take any oral medications. You must be nil by mouth (NPO) in case emergency surgery is needed — eating or drinking increases the risk of dangerous aspiration of stomach contents during general anaesthesia. Do NOT apply a heat pad to the abdomen — can accelerate rupture. Do NOT take laxatives or enemas. Seek emergency medical care immediately and inform medical staff of the exact time of your last food and drink.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How long does recovery take after appendectomy?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Laparoscopic (uncomplicated): hospital discharge in 1-2 days; return to light activities in 1-2 weeks; full recovery and return to manual work at 4-6 weeks. Open appendectomy (uncomplicated): hospital 2-4 days; light activities at 2-3 weeks; full recovery 6-8 weeks. Perforated appendicitis with peritonitis: hospital stay 5-14 days or more; full recovery 4-8 weeks depending on complications. Post-operative fatigue is normal — allow adequate rest and do not rush recovery.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can appendicitis come back after surgery?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: After complete appendectomy (total removal), appendicitis cannot recur — the appendix is gone. However, stump appendicitis can occur if a segment of appendix longer than 5mm is inadvertently left behind (rare). Additionally, 5-10% of patients have persistent or recurrent right lower quadrant pain after appendectomy (post-appendectomy syndrome) from adhesions, missed diagnosis, or co-existing conditions (Crohn's disease, IBS, ovarian cysts) — these require further investigation.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How is appendicitis different in children compared to adults?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Appendicitis in children — especially under 5 years — is more dangerous than in adults. Young children cannot localize and communicate their pain clearly; symptoms are vague; fever is often higher; diarrhea is more common. Crucially, the perforation rate in children under 5 is 40-70% (vs 20-30% in adults) because diagnosis is delayed. Lymphoid hyperplasia triggered by viral infection is the most common cause in children. Any child with persistent abdominal pain, fever, and anorexia should be evaluated urgently by a paediatric surgeon.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the Alvarado score for appendicitis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The Alvarado score (also called MANTRELS) is a clinical scoring system to assess the probability of appendicitis. It scores: migration of pain to RLQ (1 point), anorexia (1), nausea/vomiting (1), RLQ tenderness (2), rebound tenderness (1), elevated temperature (1), leukocytosis >10,000/µL (2), and shift to left/neutrophilia (1) — total 10 points. Score 1-4: appendicitis unlikely; 5-6: equivocal (CT required); 7-10: high probability (prepare for surgery). It is a useful bedside tool but CT imaging provides definitive diagnosis.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What are the signs of appendiceal perforation?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Classic perforation signs: sudden brief dramatic relief of severe pain (pressure released as appendix ruptures) immediately followed by rapidly worsening and spreading abdominal pain across the entire abdomen. High fever (>39°C), board-like rigid abdomen with extreme tenderness, inability to move without severe pain, and signs of sepsis (rapid heart rate, falling blood pressure, pallor). This is a life-threatening emergency — call emergency services (999/112/911) immediately.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What tests are done to diagnose appendicitis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Diagnosis combines clinical assessment + blood tests + imaging. Blood tests: CBC (leukocytosis, neutrophilia), CRP (elevated), bilirubin (suggests perforation), pregnancy test (mandatory in women of childbearing age). Imaging: Ultrasound (first-line — especially in children and pregnant women); CT abdomen/pelvis (gold standard in adults — >95% sensitivity); MRI (preferred in pregnancy if US inconclusive). Clinical scoring tools (Alvarado score) are also used. Diagnosis should not be delayed awaiting a single test — clinical judgment is paramount.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I eat before going to hospital if I think I have appendicitis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: NO — absolutely do not eat or drink anything if appendicitis is suspected. You must remain nil by mouth (NPO — nothing per oral) because surgery requiring general anaesthesia may be needed urgently. Eating or drinking with a full stomach significantly increases the risk of aspiration (inhalation of stomach contents into the lungs) during anaesthesia — a life-threatening complication called Mendelson's syndrome. Go to the emergency department immediately and tell staff the exact time you last ate or drank.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Does a high-fibre diet help prevent appendicitis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Epidemiological evidence suggests that populations consuming high-fibre diets have lower rates of appendicitis. Dietary fibre reduces constipation and fecalith (hardened stool) formation — the primary identifiable cause of appendiceal obstruction in adults. However, no clinical trial has confirmed that dietary changes directly prevent appendicitis. A high-fibre diet (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes — 25-30g/day) promotes overall gut health and reduces constipation, which is the best dietary preventive measure available.
